contribution: Power is the rate at which energy is transformed or transferred, $P = \Delta E : \Delta t$, and energy in kilowatt-hours is power in kilowatts times time in hours: an electricity bill is explained by the power of a device and its usage time without the concept of work.
learn: You can calculate power, energy or time with the formula $P = E : t$.
You can explain why an electricity bill depends on both power and time.
You can calculate electrical energy in kilowatt-hours and its cost.
prior: Energy is measured in joules, and it is transformed from one form to another (chapter *Energy transformations and the joule*)
Energy is neither created nor destroyed (chapter *Forms of energy and conservation of energy*)

activities.text: In the kitchen a kettle hums and the water heats up in a couple of minutes. At the same time a small lamp is burning in the hallway, and nobody needs its light. The reading of the electricity meter rises because of both, but it rises clearly faster because of the kettle. Still, the lamp is often on for hours, while the kettle is on only for a moment.
activities.question: Which uses more electrical energy, a device that works fast or a device that is on for a long time, and how can you compare them?

activities.title: Review: energy and the joule
activities.prompt: A lamp transforms electrical energy into light and heat. Which statement is correct (chapter *Energy transformations and the joule*)?

choices.text: Electrical energy disappears when the lamp is on.
choices.feedback: Energy does not disappear. In the chapter *Forms of energy and conservation of energy* we agreed that energy only changes into another form: in a lamp electrical energy changes into light and heat.

choices.text: Energy is measured in joules, and electrical energy is transformed into other forms of energy in the lamp.
choices.feedback: Correct. The unit of energy is the joule (J), and the total energy is conserved: electrical energy is transformed into light and heat. Today we add time: how fast this transformation happens.

choices.text: The joule is the rate at which energy is transformed.
choices.feedback: The joule is a unit of energy, not of rate. The rate is given by a new quantity, power, whose unit is joule per second.

activities.title: Prediction: how long the lamp has to burn
activities.prompt: The power of a hair dryer is $1800\,\text{W}$, and it is used for $5.0\,\text{min}$. The power of the hallway lamp is $10\,\text{W}$. How long does the lamp have to burn to transform the same amount of electrical energy as the dryer?

choices.text: About $5\,\text{min}$, because the energy has to build up in the same time.
choices.feedback: In the same time the lamp transforms only $10\,\text{J/s} \cdot 300\,\text{s} = 3000\,\text{J}$, while the dryer transforms $1800\,\text{J/s} \cdot 300\,\text{s} = 540\,000\,\text{J}$. The power of the lamp is small, so much more time is needed.

choices.text: About $1\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: In an hour the lamp transforms $10\,\text{J/s} \cdot 3600\,\text{s} = 36\,000\,\text{J}$, which is less than a tenth of the dryer's $540\,000\,\text{J}$. Clearly more time is needed.

choices.text: About $15\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: Correct: the power of the lamp is 180 times smaller than that of the dryer, so 180 times more time is needed than $300\,\text{s}$, which is $54\,000\,\text{s} = 15\,\text{h}$. As a calculation $t = E : P = 540\,000\,\text{J} : 10\,\text{W}$.

choices.text: About $150\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: In that time the lamp would transform $10\,\text{J/s} \cdot 540\,000\,\text{s} = 5\,400\,000\,\text{J}$, ten times the energy of the dryer. The time needed is a tenth of this.

activities.title: Energy meter readings
activities.source_note: Laskettu laitteiden nimellistehoista (vedenkeitin $2000\,\text{W}$, tosteri $1000\,\text{W}$, televisio $80\,\text{W}$); esimerkkiaineisto, ei mittaus.
activities.text:
An energy meter is connected to three devices, and the reading is recorded every $20\,\text{s}$. The table shows the meter reading in kilojoules ($\text{kJ}$) after the device is switched on.

| $t$ (s) | kettle | toaster | television |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $0$ | $0$ | $0$ | $0$ |
| $20$ | $40$ | $20$ | $1.6$ |
| $40$ | $80$ | $40$ | $3.2$ |
| $60$ | $120$ | $60$ | $4.8$ |

The reading grows steadily. Plotted against time, the readings form a straight line whose steepness can be read from the table.

question.prompt: From which numbers in the table can you see how fast the toaster transforms energy?

choices.text: From the reading $60\,\text{kJ}$, because it is the greatest energy of the toaster.
choices.feedback: The reading $60\,\text{kJ}$ only tells how much energy has been transformed in $60\,\text{s}$. The rate is found when the energy is divided by time.

choices.text: From the increase in energy divided by time: $20\,\text{kJ}$ in each interval of $20\,\text{s}$, that is $1000\,\text{J}$ per second.
choices.feedback: Correct. The increase in energy $\Delta E = 20\,000\,\text{J}$ divided by the time $\Delta t = 20\,\text{s}$ is $1000\,\text{J/s} = 1000\,\text{W}$. The same quotient is found from any interval, because the growth is steady.

choices.text: From the time $60\,\text{s}$, because a long time means a high power.
choices.feedback: Time alone does not tell the power. Power is energy per unit of time: the same power produces more energy all the time.

activities.title: The energy of the lamp over time
activities.source_note: Laskettu lampun nimellistehosta $10\,\text{W}$ ja kuivaimen tehosta $1800\,\text{W}$; esimerkkiaineisto, ei mittaus.
activities.text:
In $5.0\,\text{min}$ a hair dryer transforms $0.54\,\text{MJ}$ of electrical energy. The table shows the energy transformed by a $10\,\text{W}$ lamp when it burns continuously.

| time | energy of the lamp (MJ) |
| --- | --- |
| $1\,\text{h}$ | $0.036$ |
| $5\,\text{h}$ | $0.18$ |
| $24\,\text{h}$ | $0.86$ |

The power of the lamp is the same $10\,\text{W}$ all the time. Still, the energy it transforms grows with time.

question.prompt: Calculate how long the lamp has to burn to have transformed the same energy as the dryer in five minutes. Check the result against the table.

choices.text: Five minutes, because the energy has to build up in the same time.
choices.feedback: In the same time the lamp transforms only $10\,\text{W} \cdot 300\,\text{s} = 3000\,\text{J}$, because its power is small. At a low power the same energy takes much longer.

choices.text: About $15\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: Correct: $t = E : P = 540\,000\,\text{J} : 10\,\text{W} = 54\,000\,\text{s} = 15\,\text{h}$. Check against the table: $15\,\text{h}$ is between the rows $5\,\text{h}$ ($0.18\,\text{MJ}$) and $24\,\text{h}$ ($0.86\,\text{MJ}$), and $0.54\,\text{MJ}$ is between them.

choices.text: About $5\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: In five hours the lamp has transformed only $0.18\,\text{MJ}$, a third of the dryer's $0.54\,\text{MJ}$.

choices.text: About $24\,\text{h}$.
choices.feedback: In $24\,\text{h}$ the lamp transforms $0.86\,\text{MJ}$, which is more than the dryer's $0.54\,\text{MJ}$. The same energy is reached earlier, when you calculate $t = E : P$.

activities.title: Conclusion: power and time
activities.prompt: Write, based on the tables: why can a $10\,\text{W}$ lamp transform more energy than a $1800\,\text{W}$ hair dryer? How do power and time together determine the energy transformed?
activities.model: Power tells how much energy is transformed per second: $1800\,\text{J}$ for the dryer and $10\,\text{J}$ for the lamp. The energy transformed is power times time, so a small power is enough when there is a lot of time: in a day the lamp transforms $0.86\,\text{MJ}$ and the dryer in five minutes $0.54\,\text{MJ}$. The lamp has to burn for about $15\,\text{h}$ to reach the dryer's five-minute energy. The numbers have been calculated from rated powers, not measured.
criteria: I said in words that power is energy per second.
I used the equation $E = P\,t$ and took time into account.
I justified with numerical values that the lamp transforms more.
I remembered that the numbers are calculated from rated powers.

activities.title: Return to your prediction
activities.prompt: Compare your prediction with the numbers $E = P\,t$. What does power tell and what does it not tell? Return to the opening question: why can you not work out an electricity bill from the power alone?

activities.title: Find the error
activities.prompt: A student calculates what a $1500\,\text{W}$ heater costs when it is on for $3.0\,\text{h}$ and the price is $20\,\text{c/kWh}$. They write $E = 1500 \cdot 3.0\,\text{kWh} = 4500\,\text{kWh}$ and the cost $4500 \cdot 0.20\,\text{€} = 900\,\text{€}$. Where is the error?

choices.text: The power was not converted to kilowatts: correct is $E = 1.5\,\text{kW} \cdot 3.0\,\text{h} = 4.5\,\text{kWh}$, and the cost is $0.90\,\text{€}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. You get kilowatt-hours only when the power is in kilowatts: $1500\,\text{W} = 1.5\,\text{kW}$. The error also shows up in the reasonableness check: $900\,\text{€}$ for three hours of heating would be impossible.

choices.text: The time should have been converted to seconds before the calculation.
choices.feedback: Seconds are needed when energy is calculated in joules. For kilowatt-hours the time in hours is fine, as long as the power is in kilowatts. The error is in the unit of power.

choices.text: The cost should be divided by three, because the heater was on for three hours.
choices.feedback: The three hours are already included in the energy. Dividing would not fix the error: the result would still be far from the correct $0.90\,\text{€}$, because the power was left in watts.

choices.text: There is no error in the calculation.
choices.feedback: The result $900\,\text{€}$ is impossible: three hours of heating would cost more than a month of electricity. The power was left in watts, although kWh needs kilowatts.

activities.title: Standby for a year
activities.prompt: A television and a game console are on standby with a total power of $2.5\,\text{W}$ for the whole year, $365\,\text{days}$. How much energy does this consume in a year? Give the answer in kilowatt-hours.
hints: Is the power constant? How many hours are there in a year?
Use $E = P\,t$. Convert the power to kilowatts so that the result comes out in kilowatt-hours.

mistakes.feedback: The power was left in watts. For kilowatt-hours $2.5\,\text{W} = 0.0025\,\text{kW}$; the result 21 900 would be watt-hours.
You used $365\,\text{h}$ as the time. A year has $365\,\text{days}$, that is $365 \cdot 24\,\text{h} = 8760\,\text{h}$.

activities.solution:
**Given:** power $P = 2.5\,\text{W}$ (constant), time $365\,\text{days}$

**Find:** energy $E$ in kilowatt-hours

**Principle:** The standby power is steady, so the energy transformed is power times time.

**Formula:** $E = P\,t$

**Conversions:** $2.5\,\text{W} = 2.5 \cdot 10^{-3}\,\text{kW} = 0.0025\,\text{kW}$ (substituting $1\,\text{W} = 10^{-3}\,\text{kW}$) and $365\,\text{days} = 365 \cdot 24\,\text{h} = 8760\,\text{h}$.

**Substitution:** $E = 0.0025\,\text{kW} \cdot 8760\,\text{h} = 21.9\,\text{kWh}$

**Answer:** $22\,\text{kWh}$, two significant figures as in the power $2.5\,\text{W}$.

**Reasonableness:** In a day about $2.5\,\text{W} \cdot 24\,\text{h} = 60\,\text{Wh} = 0.06\,\text{kWh}$ is consumed, and in $365\,\text{days}$ about $22\,\text{kWh}$. The cost would be about $22 \cdot 0.20\,\text{€} \approx 4.4\,\text{€}$: small but pointless.

activities.text: Practise at three levels. Level 1 tasks use the formula $P = E : t$ directly, level 2 tasks convert units and calculate prices, and level 3 requires reasoning.

activities.title: 1. Concept
activities.prompt: Device A is on at a power of $500\,\text{W}$ for four hours. Device B is on at a power of $1500\,\text{W}$ for one hour. Which one transforms more electrical energy?

choices.text: Device B, because its power is greater.
choices.feedback: Power alone does not decide. Device B transforms $1.5\,\text{kW} \cdot 1\,\text{h} = 1.5\,\text{kWh}$, but device A transforms in its longer time $0.5\,\text{kW} \cdot 4\,\text{h} = 2.0\,\text{kWh}$.

choices.text: Device A, because $0.5\,\text{kW} \cdot 4\,\text{h} = 2.0\,\text{kWh}$ is more than $1.5\,\text{kWh}$.
choices.feedback: Correct. Energy is power times time, and a long time compensates for a smaller power: A transforms $2.0\,\text{kWh}$ and B $1.5\,\text{kWh}$.

choices.text: The same amount, because power times time is 1500 for both.
choices.feedback: The products are not equal: $500\,\text{W} \cdot 4\,\text{h} = 2000\,\text{Wh}$ and $1500\,\text{W} \cdot 1\,\text{h} = 1500\,\text{Wh}$, so A transforms more.

activities.title: 2. Power of a washing machine
activities.prompt: A washing machine consumes $1.2\,\text{kWh}$ of energy during a wash programme of $90\,\text{min}$. What is its average power? Give the answer in watts.
hints: Power is energy divided by time. In which units must the energy and the time be for the result to be in watts?
$P = E : t$. Convert $1.2\,\text{kWh}$ to joules and $90\,\text{min}$ to seconds.

mistakes.feedback: You calculated the energy in kilowatt-hours and the time in hours, so the result is in kilowatts: $1.2\,\text{kWh} : 1.5\,\text{h} = 0.8\,\text{kW}$. The question asked for watts, so multiply by 1000.

You divided the energy given in hours by minutes ($1200\,\text{Wh} : 90\,\text{min}$). The time has to be converted to hours, $90\,\text{min} = 1.5\,\text{h}$, or the energy to joules and the time to seconds.

activities.solution:
**Given:** energy $E = 1.2\,\text{kWh}$, time $t = 90\,\text{min}$

**Find:** average power $P$ in watts

**Principle:** Power is the energy transformed divided by the time it takes; the average power describes the whole wash.

**Formula:** $P = \dfrac{E}{t}$

**Conversions:** $1.2\,\text{kWh} = 1.2 \cdot 1000\,\text{W} \cdot 3600\,\text{s} = 4\,320\,000\,\text{J}$ and $90\,\text{min} = 90 \cdot 60\,\text{s} = 5400\,\text{s}$.

**Substitution:** $P = \dfrac{4\,320\,000\,\text{J}}{5400\,\text{s}} = 800\,\dfrac{\text{J}}{\text{s}} = 800\,\text{W}$

**Answer:** $8.0 \cdot 10^{2}\,\text{W}$, two significant figures as in the energy $1.2\,\text{kWh}$.

**Reasonableness:** In kilowatt-hours and hours $1.2\,\text{kWh} : 1.5\,\text{h} = 0.8\,\text{kW} = 800\,\text{W}$. This is smaller than the $2000\,\text{W}$ of a kettle but greater than the $80\,\text{W}$ of a television, which fits a washing machine that heats water only part of the time.

activities.title: 3. Explain and transfer
activities.prompt: A family wants to reduce its electricity bill. Explain why both the power of a device and its usage time must be taken into account, and give two ways to reduce consumption.
criteria: I say that energy is power times time, $E = P\,t$.
I mention that the size of the bill depends on the amount of kWh and the price.
I give two ways: for example a lower power or a shorter usage time.
I mention standby or a small device that is on for a long time.
activities.model: An electricity bill is the energy consumed in kilowatt-hours times the price, and energy is power times time. So a high power for a short time, like a hair dryer, and a low power for a long time, like a device on standby, can consume the same amount. Consumption can be reduced by choosing a low-power device, for example an $8\,\text{W}$ LED lamp instead of a $60\,\text{W}$ incandescent bulb, or by shortening the time by switching off lights and devices that are not in use. Standby can be cut off with the power switch.

activities.text: Finally, three quick questions. Answer first yourself and only then open the answer.
